source: If to Starbuck the apparition of the Squid was a thing of portents, to Queequeg it was quite a different object.
“When you see him ’quid,” said the savage, honing his harpoon in the bow of his hoisted boat, “then you quick see him ’parm whale.”

The next day was exceedingly still and sultry, and with nothing special to engage them, the Pequod’s crew could hardly resist the spell of sleep induced by such a vacant sea. For this part of the Indian Ocean through which we then were voyaging is not what whalemen call a lively ground; that is, it affords fewer glimpses of porpoises, dolphins, flying-fish, and other vivacious denizens of more stirring waters, than those off the Rio de la Plata, or the in-shore ground off Peru.

It was my turn to stand at the foremast-head; and with my shoulders leaning against the slackened royal shrouds, to and fro I idly swayed in what seemed an enchanted air. No resolution could withstand it; in that dreamy mood losing all consciousness, at last my soul went out of my body; though my body still continued to sway as a pendulum will, long after the power which first moved it is withdrawn.

Ere forgetfulness altogether came over me, I had noticed that the seamen at the main and mizzen-mast-heads were already drowsy. So that at last all three of us lifelessly swung from the spars, and for every swing that we made there was a nod from below from the slumbering helmsman. The waves, too, nodded their indolent crests; and across the wide trance of the sea, east nodded to west, and the sun over all.

Suddenly bubbles seemed bursting beneath my closed eyes; like vices my hands grasped the shrouds; some invisible, gracious agency preserved me; with a shock I came back to life. And lo! close under our lee, not forty fathoms off, a gigantic Sperm Whale lay rolling in the water like the capsized hull of a frigate, his broad, glossy back, of an Ethiopian hue, glistening in the sun’s rays like a mirror. But lazily undulating in the trough of the sea, and ever and anon tranquilly spouting his vapory jet, the whale looked like a portly burgher smoking his pipe of a warm afternoon. But that pipe, poor whale, was thy last. As if struck by some enchanter’s wand, the sleepy ship and every sleeper in it all at once started into wakefulness; and more than a score of voices from all parts of the vessel, simultaneously with the three notes from aloft, shouted forth the accustomed cry, as the great fish slowly and regularly spouted the sparkling brine into the air.
“Clear away the boats! Luff!” cried Ahab. And obeying his own order, he dashed the helm down before the helmsman could handle the spokes.

The sudden exclamations of the crew must have alarmed the whale; and ere the boats were down, majestically turning, he swam away to the leeward, but with such a steady tranquillity, and making so few ripples as he swam, that thinking after all he might not as yet be alarmed, Ahab gave orders that not an oar should be used, and no man must speak but in whispers. So seated like Ontario Indians on the gunwales of the boats, we swiftly but silently paddled along; the calm not admitting of the noiseless sails being set. Presently, as we thus glided in chase, the monster perpendicularly flitted his tail forty feet into the air, and then sank out of sight like a tower swallowed up.

“There go flukes!” was the cry, an announcement immediately followed by Stubb’s producing his match and igniting his pipe, for now a respite was granted. After the full interval of his sounding had elapsed, the whale rose again, and being now in advance of the smoker’s boat, and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted upon the honor of the capture. It was obvious, now, that the whale had at length become aware of his pursuers. All silence of cautiousness was therefore no longer of use. Paddles were dropped, and oars came loudly into play. And still puffing at his pipe, Stubb cheered on his crew to the assault.
Yes, a mighty change had come over the fish. All alive to his jeopardy, he was going “head out”; that part obliquely projecting from the mad yeast which he brewed.*

*It will be seen in some other place of what a very light substance the entire interior of the sperm whale’s enormous head consists. Though apparently the most massive, it is by far the most buoyant part about him. So that with ease he elevates it in the air, and invariably does so when going at his utmost speed. Besides, such is the breadth of the upper part of the front of his head, and such the tapering cut-water formation of the lower part, that by obliquely elevating his head, he thereby may be said to transform himself from a bluff-bowed sluggish galliot into a sharppointed New York pilot-boat.

“Start her, start her, my men! Don’t hurry yourselves; take plenty of time—but start her; start her like thunder-claps, that’s all,” cried Stubb, spluttering out the smoke as he spoke. “Start her, now; give ’em the long and strong stroke, Tashtego. Start her, Tash, my boy—start her, all; but keep cool, keep cool—cucumbers is the word—easy, easy—only start her like grim death and grinning devils, and raise the buried dead perpendicular out of their graves, boys—that’s all. Start her!”

“Woo-hoo! Wa-hee!” screamed the Gay-Header in reply, raising some old war-whoop to the skies; as every oarsman in the strained boat involuntarily bounced forward with the one tremendous leading stroke which the eager Indian gave.
But his wild screams were answered by others quite as wild. “Kee-hee! Kee-hee!” yelled Daggoo, straining forwards and backwards on his seat, like a pacing tiger in his cage.

“Ka-la! Koo-loo!” howled Queequeg, as if smacking his lips over a mouthful of Grenadier’s steak. And thus with oars and yells the keels cut the sea. Meanwhile, Stubb retaining his place in the van, still encouraged his men to the onset, all the while puffing the smoke from his mouth. Like desperadoes they tugged and they strained, till the welcome cry was heard—“Stand up, Tashtego!—give it to him!” The harpoon was hurled. “Stern all!” The oarsmen backed water; the same moment something went hot and hissing along every one of their wrists. It was the magical line. An instant before, Stubb had swiftly caught two additional turns with it round the loggerhead, whence, by reason of its increased rapid circlings, a hempen blue smoke now jetted up and mingled with the steady fumes from his pipe. As the line passed round and round the loggerhead; so also, just before reaching that point, it blisteringly passed through and through both of Stubb’s hands, from which the hand-cloths, or squares of quilted canvas sometimes worn at these times, had accidentally dropped. It was like holding an enemy’s sharp two-edged sword by the blade, and that enemy all the time striving to wrest it out of your clutch.

“Wet the line! wet the line!” cried Stubb to the tub oarsman (him seated by the tub) who, snatching off his hat, dashed sea-water into it.* More turns were taken, so that the line began holding its place. The boat now flew through the boiling water like a shark all fins. Stubb and Tashtego here changed places—stem for stern—a staggering business truly in that rocking commotion.

*Partly to show the indispensableness of this act, it may here be stated, that, in the old Dutch fishery, a mop was used to dash the running line with water; in many other ships, a wooden piggin, or bailer, is set apart for that purpose. Your hat, however, is the most convenient.

From the vibrating line extending the entire length of the upper part of the boat, and from its now being more tight than a harpstring, you would have thought the craft had two keels—one cleaving the water, the other the air—as the boat churned on through both opposing elements at once. A continual cascade played at the bows; a ceaseless whirling eddy in her wake; and, at the slightest motion from within, even but of a little finger, the vibrating, cracking craft canted over her spasmodic gunwale into the sea. Thus they rushed; each man with might and main clinging to his seat, to prevent being tossed to the foam; and the tall form of Tashtego at the steering oar crouching almost double, in order to bring down his centre of gravity. Whole Atlantics and Pacifics seemed passed as they shot on their way, till at length the whale somewhat slackened his flight.

“Haul in—haul in!” cried Stubb to the bowsman! and, facing round towards the whale, all hands began pulling the boat up to him, while yet the boat was being towed on. Soon ranging up by his flank, Stubb, firmly planting his knee in the clumsy cleat, darted dart after dart into the flying fish; at the word of command, the boat alternately sterning out of the way of the whale’s horrible wallow, and then ranging up for another fling.

The red tide now poured from all sides of the monster like brooks down a hill. His tormented body rolled not in brine but in blood, which bubbled and seethed for furlongs behind in their wake. The slanting sun playing upon this crimson pond in the sea, sent back its reflection into every face, so that they all glowed to each other like red men. And all the while, jet after jet of white smoke was agonizingly shot from the spiracle of the whale, and vehement puff after puff from the mouth of the excited headsman; as at every dart, hauling in upon his crooked lance (by the line attached to it), Stubb straightened it again and again, by a few rapid blows against the gunwale, then again and again sent it into the whale.

“Pull up—pull up!” he now cried to the bowsman, as the waning whale relaxed in his wrath. “Pull up!—close to!” and the boat ranged along the fish’s flank. When reaching far over the bow, Stubb slowly churned his long sharp lance into the fish, and kept it there, carefully churning and churning, as if cautiously seeking to feel after some gold watch that the whale might have swallowed, and which he was fearful of breaking ere he could hook it out. But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the fish. And now it is struck; for, starting from his trance into that unspeakable thing called his “flurry,” the monster horribly wallowed in his blood, overwrapped himself in impenetrable, mad, boiling spray, so that the imperilled craft, instantly dropping astern, had much ado blindly to struggle out from that phrensied twilight into the clear air of the day.

And now abating in his flurry, the whale once more rolled out into view; surging from side to side; spasmodically dilating and contracting his spout-hole, with sharp, cracking, agonized respirations. At last, gush after gush of clotted red gore, as if it had been the purple lees of red wine, shot into the frighted air; and falling back again, ran dripping down his motionless flanks into the sea. His heart had burst!
“He’s dead, Mr. Stubb,” said Daggoo.
“Yes; both pipes smoked out!” and withdrawing his own from his mouth, Stubb scattered the dead ashes over the water; and, for a moment, stood thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made.

And all the while the whale's spout-hole shot out jet after jet of white smoke in agony, and the excited headsman's mouth shot out puff after furious puff; for after every dart Stubb hauled in his bent lance (by the line tied to it), straightened it again and again with a few quick blows against the gunwale, and then drove it into the whale again and again.

"Pull up — pull up!" he now cried to the bowsman, as the waning whale slackened in his wrath. "Pull up! — close to!" And the boat drew up along the fish's flank. Then, reaching far over the bow, Stubb slowly churned his long sharp lance into the fish, and kept it there, carefully churning and churning, as if cautiously feeling for some gold watch that the whale might have swallowed, and which he was afraid of breaking before he could hook it out. But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the fish. And now it is struck; for, starting from his trance into that unspeakable thing called his "flurry," the monster wallowed horribly in his blood and wrapped himself in impenetrable, mad, boiling spray, so that the endangered boat, instantly dropping astern, had a hard time struggling blindly out of that frenzied twilight into the clear air of the day.

And now, his flurry subsiding, the whale once more rolled into view, surging from side to side, spasmodically expanding and contracting his spout-hole with sharp, cracking, agonized breaths. At last, gush after gush of clotted red gore, as if it were the purple dregs of red wine, shot into the frightened air, and falling back again, ran dripping down his motionless flanks into the sea. His heart had burst!
"He's dead, Mr. Stubb," said Daggoo.
"Yes — both pipes smoked out!" And withdrawing his own pipe from his mouth, Stubb scattered the dead ashes over the water, and for a moment stood thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 61 — Stubb dræber en hval
paragraphs: Hvis Starbuck så Blæksprutteens syn som et varsel, så Queequeg det som noget ganske andet.
»Når du ser ham blæksprutte,« sagde vilden og sleb sin harpun i stævnen på sin hejste båd, »så du hurtig se ham kaskelot.«

Den næste dag var overordentlig stille og lummer, og da de ikke havde noget særligt at tage sig til, kunne Pequods mandskab næppe modstå søvnens trylleri, som et så tomt hav fremkaldte. For den del af Det Indiske Ocean, vi dengang sejlede igennem, er ikke, hvad hvalfangere kalder et levende fangstfelt, det vil sige, at man ser færre marsvin, delfiner, flyvefisk og andre livlige beboere af travlere farvande end på fangstfelterne ud for Rio de la Plata eller kystfeltet ud for Peru.

Det var min tur til at stå vagt i fokkemastens top, og med skuldrene læsset mod de slappe royalvanter svajede jeg dovent frem og tilbage i det, der føltes som fortryllet luft. Ingen beslutning kunne holde stand mod den. Jeg mistede al bevidsthed i den drømmende stemning, og til sidst forlod min sjæl min krop, selv om min krop blev ved med at svaje, som et pendul gør længe efter, at den kraft, der satte det i gang, er forsvundet.

Før jeg helt tabte mig selv, havde jeg lagt mærke til, at mændene i stormasten og mesanmasten allerede var søvnige. Så til sidst hang vi alle tre og svingede livløst fra rærne, og for hvert sving, vi gjorde, nikkede den døsende rorgænger nedenunder. Bølgerne nikkede også med deres dovne toppe, og hen over havets vide trance nikkede øst til vest, og solen over alt.

Pludselig var det, som om bobler sprang under mine lukkede øjenlåg. Mine hænder klamrede sig til vanterne som skruestikker. En eller anden usynlig, barmhjertig magt reddede mig, og med et sæt kom jeg til live igen. Og se! Tæt under vores læ, ikke fyrre favne væk, lå en kæmpemæssig kaskelot og væltede sig i vandet som skroget af en kæntret fregat, med sin brede, blanke ryg, farvet som en etiopiers, skinnende i solen som et spejl. Mens den vuggede dovent i bølgedalen og roligt sendte sin tågede stråle op en gang imellem, lignede hvalen en tyk borger, der ryger sin pibe en varm eftermiddag. Men den pibe, stakkels hval, var din sidste. Som rørt af en tryllekunstners stav vågnede det døsende skib og hver eneste sovende om bord i ét nu. Og mere end tyve stemmer fra alle dele af fartøjet, sammen med de tre råb fra oven, løftede det velkendte råb, mens den store fisk langsomt og jævnt sprøjtede det funklende saltvand op i luften.
»Klar bådene! Luv op!« råbte Ahab. Og han adlød sin egen ordre og slog roret ned, før rorgængeren kunne nå rattet.

Mandskabets pludselige råb må have forskrækket hvalen, for før bådene var nede, vendte den majestætisk om og svømmede til læ — men så jævnt og roligt og med så få krusninger, at Ahab, der tænkte, at den måske alligevel ikke var forskrækket endnu, befalede, at ingen åre måtte bruges, og at ingen måtte tale højere end en hvisken. Så vi sad på esingerne som indianerne ved Ontario og padlede hurtigt, men lydløst af sted. Vindstille gjorde det umuligt at sætte de lydløse sejl. Snart, mens vi gled efter den på den måde, kastede uhyret sin hale lige op i luften, fyrre fod højt, og sank derefter af syne som et tårn, der sluges af jorden.

»Der går halen!« lød råbet — en melding, som straks blev fulgt af, at Stubb tog sin tændstik frem og tændte sin pibe, for nu var der givet et åndehul. Da hele tiden for dens dykning (dens dybe dyk) var gået, steg hvalen op igen, og da den nu var foran røgerens båd og meget nærmere den end nogen af de andre, regnede Stubb med æren af fangsten. Det var nu tydeligt, at hvalen endelig var blevet opmærksom på sine forfølgere. Al forsigtig tavshed var derfor ikke længere til nogen nytte. Padlerne blev smidt, og årerne kom højlydt i brug. Og stadig pustende på sin pibe opmuntrede Stubb sit mandskab til angrebet.
Ja, en vældig forandring var kommet over fisken. Fuldt bevidst om sin fare gik den »med hovedet ude«, hovedet stikkende skråt op fra den vanvittige gær, den brygger.*

*Det vil andetsteds ses, af hvilket meget let stof hele det indre af kaskelottens enorme hoved består. Selv om det tilsyneladende er det mest massive, er det langt den letteste del af den. Så den løfter det op i luften med lethed og gør det altid, når den går med sin højeste fart. Desuden er den øvre del af hovedets front så bred, og den nedre del så tilspidset og stævnformet, at man ved at løfte hovedet skråt kan sige, at den forvandler sig fra en butstævnet, tung galiot (et bredt hollandsk fragtskib) til en spidsstævnet newyorksk lodsbåd.

»Sæt i, sæt i, mine drenge! Ingen hast — tag god tid — men sæt i, sæt i, så det tordner, det er det hele,« råbte Stubb og sprutede røg ud, mens han talte. »Sæt i nu, giv dem det lange, stærke tag, Tashtego. Sæt i, Tash, min dreng — sæt i, alle sammen, men hold hovedet koldt, hold hovedet koldt — agurker er parolen — rolig, rolig — bare sæt i som den grimme død og grinende djævle og rejs de begravede døde lige op af deres grave, drenge — det er det hele. Sæt i!«

»Hu-hu! Wa-hii!« skreg Gay Head-indianeren til svar og sendte et gammelt krigsråb op mod himlen, mens hver roer i den anstrengte båd uvilkårligt kastede sig fremad i det ene vældige hovedtag, som den ivrige indianer gav.
Men hans vilde skrig blev besvaret af andre lige så vilde. »Ki-hi! Ki-hi!« hylede Daggoo og kastede sig frem og tilbage på sit sæde som en tiger, der går frem og tilbage i sit bur.

»Ka-la! Ku-lu!« brølede Queequeg, som om han smaskede over en mundfuld grenaderbøf. Og sådan skar kølene gennem havet, med årer og skrig. Imens holdt Stubb sin plads forrest og drev stadig sine mænd frem mod angrebet, mens han hele tiden pustede røg ud af munden. Som desperadoer sled og slæbte de, indtil det kærkomne råb lød — »Op med dig, Tashtego! — giv ham den!« Harpunen blev slynget. »Bak alle!« Roerne bakkede, og i samme øjeblik gik der noget varmt og hvislende hen over hver eneste af deres håndled. Det var den magiske line. Et øjeblik før havde Stubb hurtigt taget to ekstra tørn med den om klampen (stolpen agter i båden, som linen holdes an om), hvorfra der på grund af den stadig hurtigere omløben nu sprøjtede en blå røg af hamp op, som blandede sig med de jævne dampe fra hans pibe. Som linen gik rundt og rundt om klampen, gik den lige før det punkt også svidende igen og igen gennem begge Stubbs hænder, hvorfra håndklæderne — firkanter af stoppet sejldug, som man somme tider bærer ved den slags lejligheder — ved et uheld var faldet af. Det var som at holde en fjendes skarpe tveæggede sværd i bladet, mens fjenden hele tiden kæmper for at vriste det ud af ens greb.

»Væd linen! Væd linen!« råbte Stubb til tøndeårsmanden (den, der sad ved tønden), som flåede hatten af og øste havvand i den.* Der blev taget flere tørn, så linen begyndte at holde sin plads. Båden fløj nu gennem det kogende vand som en haj, der består af ren finne. Stubb og Tashtego byttede her plads — stavn for agter — en svimlende affære i al den slingrende uro.

*Dels for at vise, hvor uundværlig denne handling er, kan det nævnes her, at man i det gamle hollandske fangstfiskeri brugte en svaber til at øse vand på den løbende line; på mange andre skibe er der sat en træspand, eller et øsekar, til side til det formål. Din hat er dog den mest bekvemme.

Af den dirrende line, der strakte sig langs hele den øvre del af båden, og af at den nu var strammere end en harpestreng, kunne man have troet, at fartøjet havde to køle — den ene kløvede vandet, den anden luften — mens båden pløjede videre gennem begge modstridende elementer på én gang. Ved stævnen spillede der en uafbrudt kaskade, i kølvandet en uophørlig hvirvlende strøm, og ved den mindste bevægelse indefra, selv bare med en lillefinger, vippede det dirrende, knagende fartøj sin krampagtige essing ud i havet. Sådan stormede de af sted. Hver mand klamrede sig af alle kræfter til sit sæde for ikke at blive slynget ud i skummet, og Tashtegos høje skikkelse ved styreåren duckede sig næsten dobbelt for at få sit tyngdepunkt ned. Hele Atlanterhave og Stillehave syntes at fare forbi, mens de skød af sted, indtil hvalen til sidst en smule slækkede sin flugt.

»Hal ind — hal ind!« råbte Stubb til stævnmanden. Og mens de vendte ansigtet mod hvalen, begyndte alle mand at hale båden op til den, mens båden stadig blev slæbt af sted. Snart nåede de op langs dens flanke, og Stubb satte knæet fast i den klodsede knæholder og stak lanse efter lanse ind i den flygtende fisk. På kommando bakkede båden skiftevis ud af rækkevidde af hvalens frygtelige rullen og kom så op igen til et nyt kast.

Nu væltede den røde strøm ud fra monstrets sider på alle kanter som bække, der løber ned ad en skråning. Dets pinte krop rullede ikke i saltvand, men i blod, som boblede og kogte over flere furlong bag dem. Den lave sol, der legede over denne karmosinrøde dam i havet, kastede sit genskin tilbage i hvert eneste ansigt, så mændene alle glødede mod hinanden som rødhuder. Og hele tiden skød hvalens pusthul stråle efter stråle af hvid damp ud i smerte, og den ophidsede bådførers mund skød det ene ophidsede pust efter det andet ud; for efter hvert kast halede Stubb sin bøjede lanse ind (i linen, der var bundet til den), rettede den ud igen og igen med nogle hurtige slag mod essingen og drev den så ind i hvalen igen og igen.

»Hal op — hal op!« råbte han nu til stævnmanden, da den svækkede hval slækkede sin vrede. »Hal op! — tæt på!« Og båden kom op langs fiskens flanke. Så lænede Stubb sig langt ud over stævnen og rørte langsomt sin lange, skarpe lanse rundt inde i fisken og blev ved med at holde den der, omhyggeligt rørende og rørende, som om han forsigtigt famlede efter et guldur, som hvalen måske havde slugt, og som han var bange for at ødelægge, før han kunne få det op på krogen. Men det guldur, han ledte efter, var fiskens inderste liv. Og nu er det ramt; for hvalen vågnede af sin døs ind i den ubeskrivelige ting, man kalder dens »dødskamp«, og uhyret væltede sig rædsomt i sit blod og svøbte sig i uigennemtrængelig, gal, kogende sprøjt, så den udsatte båd, som straks faldt agterud, havde vanskeligt ved at kæmpe sig blindt ud af det rasende tusmørke og ind i dagens klare luft.

Og nu, da dødskampen var ved at fortage sig, rullede hvalen endnu en gang frem for øjnene af dem, vuggende fra side til side, mens den krampagtigt udvidede og trak sit pusthul sammen med skarpe, knagende, pinefulde åndedrag. Til sidst skød strøm efter strøm af størknet rødt blod, som var det de purpurfarvede bundfald af rødvin, op i den forskrækkede luft, og faldt tilbage igen og løb drivende ned ad dens ubevægelige flanker ned i havet. Dens hjerte var sprunget!
»Den er død, Mr. Stubb,« sagde Daggoo.
»Ja — begge piber er røget ud!« Og Stubb tog sin egen pibe ud af munden, spredte den døde aske ud over vandet og stod et øjeblik og betragtede eftertænksomt det vældige lig, han havde frembragt.
